# 6. Input and output

<!-- Generated by tools/generate-docs.lisp from docs/manual/chapters.lisp,
     docs/manual/introduction.md and the examples: do not edit by hand. -->

Ports read and write strings, files, and the standard streams; a program can be
spread over several files, and can load cog-lisp's own libraries from anywhere.

## Reading and writing strings as streams

`examples/string-ports.lisp`:

```scheme
; Reading characters one at a time: a tiny tokenizer for arithmetic.
(define (tokenize text)
  (let ((in (open-input-string text)))
    (let loop ((tokens '()))
      (let ((c (peek-char in)))
        (cond ((eof-object? c) (reverse tokens))
              ((char-whitespace? c) (read-char in) (loop tokens))
              ((char-numeric? c)
               (let digits ((n 0))
                 (let ((d (peek-char in)))
                   (if (and (not (eof-object? d)) (char-numeric? d))
                       (begin (read-char in) (digits (+ (* n 10) (digit-value d))))
                       (loop (cons n tokens))))))
              (else (read-char in) (loop (cons (string->symbol (string c)) tokens))))))))
(write (tokenize "12 + 3*(45 - 6)"))
(newline)

; read takes whole datums from a port, then the end-of-file object.
(define data (open-input-string "(name \"Ada\") (born 1815) 42"))
(let loop ((x (read data)))
  (unless (eof-object? x)
    (write x)
    (newline)
    (loop (read data))))

; Lines.
(define lines (open-input-string "first line\nsecond line\n"))
(write (list (read-line lines) (read-line lines) (eof-object? (read-line lines))))
(newline)

; Writing to a string.
(define out (open-output-string))
(write-string "total: " out)
(write (+ 1 2 3) out)
(write-char #\! out)
(write (get-output-string out))
(newline)
(write (with-output-to-string (lambda () (display "captured ") (display '(a b)))))
(newline)
```

Its output:

```text
(12 + 3 * ( 45 - 6 ))
(name "Ada")
(born 1815)
42
("first line" "second line" #t)
"total: 6!"
"captured (a b)"
```

## Reading and writing files with ports

A relative path names a file beside this program, wherever it is run from.

`examples/files.lisp`:

```scheme
(define scores '(("ada" 98) ("grace" 95) ("alan" 87)))

; Write a small CSV file: one line per row.
(call-with-output-file "scores.csv"
  (lambda (out)
    (for-each (lambda (row)
                (write-string (car row) out)
                (write-char #\, out)
                (write (car (cdr row)) out)
                (newline out))
              scores)))
(display (file-exists? "scores.csv"))
(newline)

; Read it back a line at a time, until the end-of-file object.
(define (read-rows port)
  (let loop ((rows '()))
    (let ((line (read-line port)))
      (if (eof-object? line)
          (reverse rows)
          (let ((fields (string-split line #\,)))
            (loop (cons (list (car fields) (string->number (car (cdr fields)))) rows)))))))
(define rows (call-with-input-file "scores.csv" read-rows))
(write rows)
(newline)
(display (equal? rows scores))
(newline)

; with-output-to-file sends display and write to the file.
(with-output-to-file "scores.csv"
  (lambda () (write '(total 280)) (newline)))
(write (call-with-input-file "scores.csv" read))      ; read a datum back
(newline)

(delete-file "scores.csv")
(display (file-exists? "scores.csv"))
(newline)
(display (guard (e ((file-error? e) (error-object-message e)))
  (open-input-file "no-such-file.txt")))
(newline)
```

Its output:

```text
#t
(("ada" 98) ("grace" 95) ("alan" 87))
#t
(total 280)
#f
open-input-file: file not found: no-such-file.txt
```

## Reading stdin from a program

Try: echo hello | cog-lisp.bat examples\echo.lisp
read-line, read-char and read with no port read the program's input.

`examples/echo.lisp`:

```scheme
(let loop ((n 1))
  (let ((line (read-line)))
    (unless (eof-object? line)
      (display n)
      (display ": ")
      (display (string-upcase line))
      (newline)
      (loop (+ n 1)))))
(display "end of input")
(newline)
```

Its input:

```text
hello
second line
```

Its output:

```text
1: HELLO
2: SECOND LINE
end of input
```

## A program in two files

Run it as: cog-lisp.bat examples\program\main.lisp alpha beta
load finds lib/util.lisp beside this file, wherever the program is run from.

`examples/program/main.lisp`:

```scheme
(load "lib/util.lisp")

(display (string-append "this file: " (file-name (current-load-path))))
(newline)
(display "arguments: ")
(write (cdr (command-line)))                       ; the program itself comes first
(newline)
(for-each (lambda (arg) (display (shout arg)) (newline))
          (cdr (command-line)))
```

`examples/program/lib/util.lisp`:

```scheme
; The last part of a path, on Windows or Linux:
; "C:\a\b\main.lisp" or "/a/b/main.lisp" -> "main.lisp"
(define (file-name path)
  (let loop ((i (- (string-length path) 1)))
    (cond ((< i 0) path)
          ((memv (string-ref path i) '(#\/ #\\)) (substring path (+ i 1) (string-length path)))
          (else (loop (- i 1))))))

(define (shout s) (string-append (string-upcase s) "!"))

(display (string-append "loaded " (file-name (current-load-path))))
(newline)
```

Run with the arguments `alpha beta`.

Its output:

```text
loaded util.lisp
this file: main.lisp
arguments: ("alpha" "beta")
ALPHA!
BETA!
```

## Require, and *env*: libraries from any folder

(load path) runs the file at a path, relative to the file that loads it.
(require 'name) is the smarter loader: it finds name.lisp in the library path
and loads it once, answering where it came from. The library path is the
folders of the COGLISP_PATH environment variable, then cog-lisp's own lib
folder, so (require 'cl) and (require 'test) work from a program anywhere.

*env* is a table of what the running world knows about itself: home (the
cog-lisp folder), library-path, libraries (what require has loaded),
platform and version. A program changes the library path with set!:
  (set! (hash-table-ref *env* 'library-path)
        (cons "my/libs" (hash-table-ref *env* 'library-path)))

`examples/libraries.lisp`:

```scheme
(define where (require 'test))
(display (string? where))                       ; the full path it loaded
(newline)
(display (string=? (require 'test) where))     ; a second require loads nothing
(newline)
(display (map car (hash-table-ref *env* 'libraries)))
(newline)
(display (string? (require-path 'cl)))          ; where it would load cl from
(newline)
(display (require-path 'no-such-library))
(newline)
(display (list? (hash-table-ref *env* 'library-path)))
(newline)
```

Its output:

```text
#t
#t
(test)
#t
#f
#t
```

## JSON: json-read and json-write

(json-read text) turns JSON text into LISP data, and (json-write value [port])
turns it back. An object is a hash table with string keys, an array a vector,
true and false are #t and #f, and null is (), the empty list (Common Lisp's
nil). JSON has no lists, so () is never anything but null. In cog-lisp only #f
is false, so test a null with null?, not with a plain if. An object's keys are
written sorted, so the same table always writes the same text.

`examples/json.lisp`:

```scheme
(define order (json-read "{\"id\": 7, \"items\": [\"tea\", \"café\"], \"paid\": false, \"note\": null}"))

(display (hash-table-ref order "id")) (newline)
(write (hash-table-ref order "items")) (newline)
(display (if (null? (hash-table-ref order "note")) "no note" "a note")) (newline)
(display (if (hash-table-ref order "paid") "paid" "not paid")) (newline)

(hash-table-set! order "paid" #t)
(json-write order) (newline)

(define summary (make-hash-table))
(hash-table-set! summary "count" (vector-length (hash-table-ref order "items")))
(hash-table-set! summary "nothing" '())
(json-write summary) (newline)
```

Its output:

```text
7
#("tea" "café")
no note
not paid
{"id":7,"items":["tea","café"],"note":null,"paid":true}
{"count":2,"nothing":null}
```
